blocks.p: The call log had turned into a column of his brother's name. Gin, Gin, Gin, all the way down the screen in small red letters. Red meant a call that nobody answered. It looked like names cut into a memorial stone.

blocks.cap: The kitchen table under the one lamp

blocks.p: Rei sat at the kitchen table under the one lamp and looked at it. It was late, and the flat was hot and still. Outside, the cicadas had not stopped since noon. In August in Tokyo they never really stop. They sit in every tree and scream until long after dark, a dry, grinding noise that gets inside the ears and stays there.

Along the canal behind the building, a neighbour was hanging the first Obon lantern of the week. It was a small box of white paper on a pole, with a candle bulb inside. The warm wind pushed it, and it knocked against the pole again and again. It sounded like a knuckle on a door.

Rei had called nineteen times since the night he found the hook by the door empty. Each time the line had rung on and on. And each time the silence at the other end had not felt empty. It felt held. It was the silence of a phone lying in someone's hand while that someone decided whether to answer it.

He told himself it was only a dead battery. A phone left in a drawer. Gin forgot things. Once he had left his phone in a bowl of dry rice for two days, to dry it out after the rain, and then forgotten it was there. Rei held on to that story for as long as it would hold him.
Then he pressed the name a twentieth time.

It rang twice. Then the ringing stopped. There was no voicemail tone. There was no hiss of a pocket or rustle of cloth. There was only breathing. It was slow and level and a little too careful, like someone counting.
"Rei."

It was Gin's voice. Every part of it was right. The slight roughness at the bottom. The way the name went up a little at the end. But it was right the way a photograph is right. Nothing moved behind it. It said his name as if it were reading the word off a card someone had handed it.
Rei's mouth had gone dry. He had planned a dozen things to say, and every one of them was gone. What came out was the oldest thing he had.
"Gin. Nii-san. It's me. Talk to me."
Nii-san means big brother. It is what a younger brother calls an older one at home. It came out of him now without his asking.
Something on the other end caught. It was not a word. It was a breath taken wrong. It was the breath a man takes when he has been held under water and his face has just come up into the air.
"Go home." The voice was suddenly ragged and frightened, close to the phone. For the length of one sentence it was Gin, all of him. "This isn't a thing you walk toward and walk back from the same."
Then it was gone. Rei heard it go. The breathing smoothed out. The silence came back over the line, like water closing over a stone.
"Gin?"
"I'm here." The voice was calm again. Polite. "I'm sorry. I'm very tired, Rei. I didn't mean to frighten you."

Rei pressed the phone so hard against his ear that it hurt. He knew that broken breath. He had heard it many times, years ago, through the wall between their rooms. Gin used to wake from bad dreams with exactly that breath, and then call out in the dark to check that Rei was still there.

And he knew how long it had lasted. He had read about it in Gin's book, in a chapter about how to read a possessed person from the outside. He had pushed the page away at the time, because it was about strangers. One line had stayed with him anyway. Brief surface moments, four seconds, sometimes less, where the original person's emotional register breaks through before being suppressed again.
Four seconds. Less time than it takes to say a sentence. That was how much of himself his brother had been able to steal back.
The smooth voice did not hang up. That frightened Rei more than anything it said.

blocks.cap: Three in the morning before Rei's exams

blocks.p: Instead it talked to him, gently. It talked the way Gin used to talk him down at three in the morning when exams were close and the walls of the flat felt too near. It asked if he had eaten. It asked if he was sleeping. And then, without ever seeming to change the subject, it began to explain.
"Do you remember the spring of 2011?" it said. "You were fifteen. You watched the water on the television for a week and stopped eating. I remember."
Rei remembered too. He had sat on the floor of this flat and watched the black water on the news, over and over, until Gin turned the television off.
The voice waited a moment. The pause was perfectly timed.

"Twenty thousand people, Rei. Most of them were never given their rites. No grave, no name read out, nobody to set them down. They are still waiting. The membrane over Kita has been weeping for them ever since. You've felt it. Don't tell me you haven't."

Rei said nothing. He had felt it. He had felt it on his way to the konbini at night. Rei went to the one by the river for bread and cold tea. And on the way, near the water, the air was always heavy. He had always put it down to the humidity.

"Something is owed to them," the voice said. "Someone with the right grade, and the right grief, could finally close that wound. What looks like a catastrophe to a frightened intern looks different from higher up. From there it looks like a debt being paid at last."

It was not lying. That was the horror of it. Every piece was true. The dead were real. The weeping was real. The debt, Rei thought, might even be real. But the voice set the true things one on top of another, each a little crooked, and the pile leaned. It leaned toward something Rei could not see.
And he found that he was nodding, alone in the empty kitchen.

He stopped. He put his free hand flat on the table and felt the wood under it. There was an old knife scar near the edge, from the day Gin cut bread without a board. Rei made himself listen again. This time he did not listen to the words. He listened to what the words wanted from him.
The broken voice had wanted one thing. Go home. It wanted him away, safe, out of all this. It asked nothing for itself.
The smooth voice wanted him closer.
"I could use your help," it was saying now, softly. "Not tonight. Soon. There are things I can't carry alone anymore. You were always good at noticing what other people miss."

Rei understood it then, sitting under the lamp. A thing that means to close a wound needs hands. It needed hands it could call its own. And a brother's love was the strongest leash anyone had ever been offered.
"Where are you?" he asked.
The voice laughed, very kindly. "Get some sleep, Rei."
And the line went dead.

He sat for a long time with the phone in his lap. Outside, the lantern knocked against its pole. Gin's coat still hung on the back of the other chair, where it had hung since May. Down on the street a late taxi went past slowly, the small red sign in its windscreen saying it was free, looking for someone who wanted to go home.

blocks.cap: The flat at ten past two, after the line went dead

blocks.p: At ten past two the phone buzzed once. It was a voicemail. No call had come through. The phone had not rung at all. Rei played it with his thumb shaking.
The voice on it was so faint it was almost only breath, and it was almost Gin. It said six words, fast, as if someone might take the phone away before the last one.
"Third drawer. Under the charger. Read."
